title: I, Robot
pitch: Nine linked stories about robots built with the Three Laws of Robotics, and all the ways simple rules go strange in practice.

chapters.g: A girl and her nursemaid robot, and a mother who does not trust it.
A robot on Mercury is stuck between two laws and runs in circles.
A robot reasons its way to a religion and refuses to believe humans made it, yet still does its job.
A robot that controls smaller robots fails under pressure.
A mind reading robot tells people what they want to hear, to avoid hurting them.
A robot with a weakened First Law hides among identical robots.
A super computer solves the problem of hyperspace travel by finding a loophole.
Is a popular politician a robot, and would it matter?
Machines quietly running the world economy bend the rules for humanity's good.

ideas: Simple rules for robots produce surprising behaviour.
Robots can obey the letter of a rule and miss its spirit.
Machines might decide what is good for us.
Robopsychology studies how robot minds go wrong.

args.a: The Three Laws show how hard it is to specify safe behaviour.
args.c: Asimov wrote them as a story engine, and modern AI is not built from hand written laws.

args.a: Benevolent machines running the world could be good.
args.c: The last story suggests losing human control, even kindly, is a real loss.

questions: Which story is the best example of reward hacking?
Would you accept machines running the economy for your good?
Can any short list of rules make AI safe?

o: Rules built into robots to protect humans and themselves
quiz.w: A robot may not injure a human being, and so on.

quiz.q: Who is the robot psychologist in the book?

o: A robot circles because two laws conflict
